newsitem.title: UK: Bank of England renews call for higher interest rates.
newsitem.headline: Bank of England renews call for higher interest rates.

text.p: The Bank of England renewed its call for an increase in interest rates at its September 4 monetary policy meeting with finance minister Kenneth Clarke, according to minutes of the meeting published on Wednesday.
But Chancellor of the Exchequer Clarke rejected its advice and left rates unchanged at 5.75 percent.

"The Bank continued to prefer a marginally tighter policy stance now and repeated the general point that the longer a tightening was delayed, the sharper it would eventually need to be," the minutes quoted central bank governor Eddie George as saying. George told Clarke that interest rates would have to rise at some point to give a better than even chance of meeting the government's 2.5 percent target for underlying inflation, known as RPIX.

"The Bank still expected RPIX inflation to fall to below 2.5 percent over the coming months," the minutes said. But rising underlying domestic demand, beginning to feed through into output, put the inflation target "at significant risk in 1998."
"Taking all the evidence together, it would be very surprising if consumer demand did not continue to grow at well above trend," the minutes quoted George as saying.
"The real question was just how strong it would become."
Clarke has cut interest rates four times since last December, incurring the wrath of the central bank on the last occasion in June.

With a general election due by next May at the latest, the Conservative government has a strong political incentive not to raise interest rates as this would mean higher mortgage costs for millions of home-owners.
Clarke said the boom in activity forecast by some people did not appear to be materialising and inflation data remained "extremely good."
"Recent surveys were more encouraging and any risk there had been of the economy slowing significantly had diminished," Clarke said.
He agreed that consumer confidence was improving but noted that broad money supply growth, often a pointer to future inflation, had fallen back within its monitoring range.
Rising house prices were attracting attention but the evidence showed recovery was concentrated in particular sections of the market and particular areas.
"There was certainly no sign of any housing market boom," the minutes quoted Clarke as saying.
